description_full: Tennant Company, together with its subsidiaries, designs, manufactures, and markets floor cleaning equipment in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. The company offers manual and autonomous mechanized cleaning equipment for industrial and commercial use, detergent-free and other sustainable cleaning technologies, aftermarket parts and consumables, and equipment maintenance and repair services. It also provides business solutions such as financing, rental and leasing programs, and machine-to-machine asset management solutions. In addition, the company offers robotic cleaning equipment; IRIS, an asset management solution; ec-H2O NanoClean, a detergent-free cleaning solution; and ReadySpace, a rapid-drying carpet cleaning technology. It offers its products under the Tennant, Nobles, Alfa Uma Empresa Tennant, IPC, Gaomei, and Rongen brands, as well as private-label brands. The company serves retail establishments, distribution centers, factories and warehouses, public venues such as arenas and stadiums, office buildings, schools and universities, hospitals and clinics, and others. It markets its products to contract cleaners and businesses through direct sales and service organizations, as well as through a network of authorized distributors. Tennant Company was founded in 1870 and is headquartered in Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

financial_summary: Tennant Company is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.2B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 42%.

The business throws off $43M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.6×.
Management returns a meaningful 8.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 2.2% of the shares.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.52x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-9.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 7% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 0.88, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.22 vs 5y 0.85), so read it loosely.
About $11.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 35% in the 2022 bear market and 82% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $70.49 (margin of safety -1%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 35%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $41.98 to $116 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 52.6 vs 23.3 and P/FCF 28.1 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 21% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $87.75 on average, 23% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.3%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.43).
It runs a 42% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.48x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.4% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.4x net debt to EBITDA ($76.4M of cash against $273.6M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 5.6x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.3% over 3 years, 3.8% over 5 years and 4.0% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -16.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.01, a backlog worth 3% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 69%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 6, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.2%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 6 purchases and 1 sale over the past year, net $1.2M bought.
It returns 8.9% a year to shareholders (7.1% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 6.1% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 11.6% of the float, 8.5 days to cover.
people: With about 4,500 employees, each generates about $267K of revenue, 0.7x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 3.4% a year.
That works out to $10K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.3M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
